text: Every lesson so far has lived inside a single vector space: one qubit's two-dimensional state. Real quantum computers have many qubits working together, and the tool that stitches their individual spaces into one combined space is the tensor product — the single most important piece of machinery in this chapter.

If you have two separate classical bits, describing both together just means listing one next to the other — no real combining. It's tempting to guess two qubits work the same way, gluing two vectors end to end. But a qubit can be a superposition of both basis states at once, so combining two of them needs an amplitude for every possible correlation between them, not just one amplitude per qubit.

Qubit 1 has 2 basis states, and qubit 2 has 2 basis states. The combined system's basis states are every pairing of one from each: ket-zero-zero, ket-zero-one, ket-one-zero, ket-one-one — 2 times 2 equals 4 basis states, so the combined space is 4-dimensional, needing 4 independent amplitudes. Three qubits follow the same logic: 2 times 2 times 2 equals 8 dimensions.

The direct sum genuinely adds dimensions — it's what you'd use for 'either system A or system B is active, never both,' with no cross-terms possible. The tensor product is what you use when both systems exist simultaneously and need to track every possible correlation between them. Multi-qubit quantum states are always built with tensor products, never direct sums, precisely because qubits in a quantum computer coexist and can become correlated.

Next lesson computes the actual numbers: the Kronecker product formula that turns two small vectors or matrices into one larger one, worked by hand on the exact states and gates you'll use for the rest of this course.
